source.title: Fewer Tokens, Greater Scaling: Self-Adaptive Visual Bases for Efficient and Expansive Representation Learning
source.authors: S. Young; Xing-Yu Zeng; Lijian Xu

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own scaling results for vision transformers, extending scaling analysis to image models and visual token bases rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, training-token or training-compute scaling, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It cites Kaplan et al. as related work, but the rows below are its own vision-model results. Some model-by-model accuracy values in Table 1 cannot be mapped reliably from the extracted chart layout and are left out.
record.test_reason: This is a ViT token-reduction method paper. Its only results on a claim version are downstream scores rising across ViT-B, ViT-L and ViT-H (V6). Its headline 'law' links input-token bases to parameters, a different construct from loss scaling. The Table 1 accuracy-vs-FLOPs trend at 96 bases bears on V5 only loosely: it is accuracy, not loss, and no fit is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim a 'token–model scaling law', the Law of Parametric Efficiency Priority: larger ViTs need fewer image bases to reach their ceiling. They also claim the Orthogonal Filtering module cuts cost and improves generalization and robustness across vision tasks. Separately, they assert that accuracy follows a power law in FLOPs at fixed token count, but give no fit.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of language-model held-out-loss scaling. It introduces an Orthogonal Filtering module and studies ImageNet accuracy, visual-basis counts, and vision downstream benchmarks across ViT sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary with model size and image-basis count; the paper also reports resolution-dependent ImageNet accuracy for ViT-Large@91.

fits_no_version.finding: Image bases needed to saturate ImageNet accuracy fall from 139 (Tiny) to 61 (Huge) as parameters grow. The text calls this 'approximately linearly' but formalises it as C/θ^α.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision transformers, the number of input tokens needed to reach the accuracy ceiling decreases with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed ViT-B, top-1 accuracy rises with input basis count (49.1 at 16 bases to about 78 at 160) and saturates near the 77.91 full-token baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Accuracy vs input-token count follows a saturating power-like curve at fixed model size.

record.problems: The study does not measure language-model held-out loss, compute scaling, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. It reports no fitted exponents or fit-residual analysis for the original claim. Some Table 1 chart values cannot be assigned reliably from the extracted layout. Parameter counts differ across the paper's tables (for example, Table 3 and Table 8 report different counts for ViT variants). Uncertainty is reported only for the displayed ViT-Base baseline in the basis-count plot.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 model-by-model accuracy results were left out because the extracted chart layout does not reliably associate all plotted values with model and metric. Table 5 OOD results do not compare model scale. Table 7 varies image resolution rather than testing a scaling law. These appear in Sections 2.3, 3.2, and 3.4.2, respectively.

untested.parts: No held-out LM loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
No loss-based power law in vision. Table 1 reports accuracy vs log FLOPs at fixed tokens with no fitted exponent. No repeated-data, fine-tuning or video scaling.
No predictive fit of downstream performance on scale or loss; only three model sizes, with confounded token counts.

missing.what: ImageNet top-1/top-5 accuracy for ViT-Tiny to ViT-Huge at fixed 96 bases vs log FLOPs. Authors claim a power law before the ceiling; Large and Huge are about equal (~82.5), showing saturation. Values are partly legible (e.g. ViT-B 76.11).

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper; Kaplan et al. is cited only as inspiration. The downstream size comparisons confound model size with basis count and FLOPs. No uncertainty is given beyond ±0.1% on the baseline. Parameter counts are inconsistent between Table 3 and Table 8.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and training-token allocation, including how either changes with compute.
Architecture-shape effects at a fixed parameter count.
The study tests image-model accuracy and visual-basis counts against model size, not the same held-out loss scaling relation, repeated-data, fine-tuning, transfer, or video scaling.
The study reports selected vision downstream benchmarks, but does not fit or validate a predictive relationship to pretraining loss or across a broad range of tasks.
Dependence of language-model exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices and setup; disagreement between published language-model laws.
